KV cache coherence in multi-agent inference asks: when multiple agents share a prefix tree of cached key-value attention states, and any one agent asynchronously mutates its context mid-sequence (tool call return, memory injection, retrieved chunk insertion), does the cached representation still correctly reflect the causal attention mask that the model was trained to expect? The naive assumption — that prefix sharing is safe because prefixes are immutable — breaks down the moment you allow any agent to write back into a shared branch, because the cached K and V tensors were computed under a specific positional encoding and causal mask that is now stale relative to the mutated token sequence. The expert worry that beginners miss is positional encoding aliasing: in RoPE-based models, the cached K/V at position i encodes not just token identity but its absolute (or relative) position, so inserting tokens upstream of a cached suffix doesn't just invalidate logical coherence — it produces silently wrong attention scores because the model reuses position-contaminated keys against queries that now sit at shifted positions. A further subtle failure is cache branch collision under async scheduling: two agents sharing a prefix can race to extend it, and if the inference runtime doesn't enforce strict copy-on-write semantics at the trie node level, one agent's speculative extension can corrupt another's view before either generation is committed. Experts also worry about mask leakage — shared prefix nodes may carry attention patterns from agent A's private context that are now visible to agent B's decode, violating both logical isolation and, in deployed systems, security boundaries between users or roles.

RoPE encodes position by rotating the query and key vectors at each head by angle θ_i = position × ω_i, where ω_i = 10000^(−2i/d) for head dimension i — crucially, this rotation is applied at compute time and then baked into the stored K tensor, so the cached K at what was position k now literally has sinusoidal coefficients for integer k embedded in its components. When you insert a token at position k, the suffix tokens should now live at positions k+1, k+2, …, n+1, but their cached K vectors still carry rotations for k, k+1, …, n — meaning every dot product Q·K^T in the suffix will compute a relative displacement that is off by exactly one, producing attention scores that correspond to the wrong inter-token distance. The "just re-index" intuition fails because un-rotating and re-rotating requires knowing the original per-head rotation matrices and applying O(n·d) compute per layer — which is precisely the cost of recomputing the keys from scratch, eliminating the cache's value entirely. SGLang's prefix tree implementation (2024) sidesteps this by treating cached blocks as immutable once committed, refusing any mid-sequence write that would invalidate suffix positions; the only safe operation is appending to a leaf node, never inserting into an interior one. A subtler issue noted in the literature on YaRN and LongRoPE is that even approximate re-indexing — scaling positions by a constant factor — measurably degrades attention pattern fidelity at the affected layers, with perplexity increases detectable within 50–100 tokens of the mutation point. The consequence for multi-agent systems is that any architecture allowing agents to inject context (tool results, retrieved chunks) mid-sequence must either restart the KV cache from the injection point forward, or use an insertion-aware architecture like memory tokens placed only at sequence boundaries — making mid-sequence context mutation fundamentally incompatible with standard RoPE caching.

When two agents sharing a prefix tree node both attempt to append concurrently, the failure mode is trie branch aliasing under non-atomic extension: agent A reads the current leaf, begins writing its append tokens into a new child node, and agent B — seeing the same leaf as the extension point — either overwrites A's partial write or creates a sibling branch that the scheduler treats as a valid shared prefix for both agents, causing B to attend over A's private tool result as if it were shared context. This is not hypothetical: vLLM's paged attention implementation (v0.3+) uses reference-counted physical blocks, and without explicit copy-on-write triggered before the first diverging token, a race between two async decode streams extending the same virtual block can produce a state where both streams' KV pages point to the same physical block containing interleaved tokens from both agents — a corruption that is silent because the block's reference count remains valid. The deeper coherence failure is causal mask inconsistency: the shared prefix was computed under a causal mask where no token attends to future tokens, but once A's append is partially visible to B's decode, B's queries may attend to A's tokens at positions that were never part of the causal graph B was initialized with, violating the invariant that each agent's attention is closed over its own context history. Lmsys's SGLang (2024) addresses this with a fork-on-write protocol at the RadixAttention layer — any extension of a shared node atomically clones the node into a private branch before writing — but the cost is that the forked blocks are no longer shared, so memory deduplication collapses exactly at the moment of concurrent generation, the highest-memory phase. The race condition also interacts badly with speculative decoding in multi-agent settings: if a draft model generates k tokens speculatively on behalf of agent A and those tokens are optimistically written into the shared trie before verification, agent B may cache a prefix that includes A's unverified speculative tokens, and a subsequent rollback by A leaves B holding KV state derived from tokens that were never committed. The only architecturally clean solution is to enforce that shared prefix nodes are read-only after first access and that each agent's generation always begins by forking a private leaf — which recovers isolation but trades away the memory savings that motivated prefix sharing in the first place.

Re-merging two forked branches is safe only if their token sequences are byte-identical from the fork point onward — a condition that can be checked by hashing the token ID sequence, which is precisely what SGLang's RadixAttention does to determine prefix cache hits. The problem is that even if two agents happen to generate identical token suffixes (say, both call the same tool and receive the same response), their KV blocks are still not safely mergeable if any layer's K or V tensors were influenced by tokens that differed between the two branches prior to the merge point — because attention is non-local: each K/V at position j is a function of the token at j alone, but each query at position j attends over all prior positions, meaning the residual stream state entering each layer is path-dependent on the full history, not just the local token. This is the core computational property that makes re-merging provably unsafe: KV tensors are computed from hidden states, not raw token embeddings, and the hidden state at position j in branch A may differ from the hidden state at position j in branch B even if token_j is identical in both, because the preceding attention outputs — shaped by each branch's divergent history — feed into the residual that produces the Q, K, V projections at j. Formally, K_j = W_K · LayerNorm(h_j), where h_j = h_{j-1} + Attn(h_{j-1}) + FFN(...), making K_j a recursive function of all prior hidden states; two branches with identical token j but different tokens at any position i < j will produce different K_j values, making their KV blocks semantically distinct despite token-level identity. The Flash Attention and PagedAttention literature both implicitly assume this immutability — block reuse in vLLM is only ever gated on prefix token hash equality precisely because the engineers recognized that token identity is the only tractable proxy for KV identity, even though it is not a sufficient condition when hidden state histories diverge. In practice, SGLang's eviction policy therefore treats forked branches as permanently independent: there is no re-merge codepath, and the memory cost of the fork is paid until both branches are evicted, which under LRU eviction can mean the longer-lived agent holds its private blocks for the full session duration.

A shared prefix does guarantee KV-identical blocks across agents when the model is stateless and deterministic — same token IDs, same weights, same layer norm parameters, same positional encodings, same floating-point execution order — and this is the implicit contract that vLLM and SGLang both rely on when they key the cache purely on token hash. The guarantee breaks immediately under LoRA or adapter injection, where different agents may be served by different adapter configurations layered onto the same base model: a LoRA adapter modifies the Q, K, V projection matrices as W + AB^T, so even with identical prefix tokens, agent A using adapter set α and agent B using adapter set β will produce different K/V tensors at every layer, making their "shared" prefix blocks physically incompatible despite token-level identity. Layer normalization with learned γ and β parameters (as in GPT-style RMSNorm or Pre-LN transformers) introduces a subtler failure: if a fine-tuned checkpoint shifts these parameters even slightly — as routinely happens in RLHF fine-tuning, where layer norm scales drift measurably across layers 16–32 in 7B-scale models — then a KV block cached under the base model's norm parameters is numerically wrong when reused under the fine-tuned model, with errors that compound multiplicatively across layers rather than additively. The S-LoRA system (Sheng et al., 2023) confronted this directly: when multiplexing hundreds of LoRA adapters on a single GPU, it found that prefix KV caches could not be shared across adapter boundaries at all, forcing per-adapter cache partitioning that significantly reduced effective cache utilization compared to single-adapter serving. A further failure mode arises with quantization skew: if agents are served at different precision levels (one at FP16, another at INT8 via GPTQ or AWQ), the KV tensors diverge due to rounding in the weight matrices, meaning a cache block computed under FP16 is not safely reusable for an INT8 agent even with identical prefix tokens and nominally identical weights. The operational implication is that true KV cache sharing requires not just token-hash matching but model-configuration identity — adapter ID, quantization scheme, norm parameter version, and inference dtype must all match — a composite cache key that most production systems either approximate crudely or ignore entirely, leaving silent numerical inconsistency as the failure mode rather than an explicit error.

During a rolling update, the inference cluster enters a split-brain cache state: workers on the old checkpoint (v_n) hold KV blocks keyed to one composite identity, workers on the new checkpoint (v_{n+1}) hold blocks keyed to another, and the load balancer — unless it is checkpoint-aware — may route successive requests from the same session to different workers, causing a request to arrive at a v_{n+1} worker expecting to extend a prefix that was cached only on a v_n worker, resulting in a full cache miss and forced recomputation from token zero. The interaction with in-flight requests is more dangerous than a simple miss: a request that began prefill on a v_n worker and cached its KV blocks mid-sequence may be rescheduled mid-generation onto a v_{n+1} worker if the original worker is drained for the update — at which point the runtime must either invalidate and recompute the entire prefix or reuse the v_n blocks under v_{n+1} weights, the latter being numerically incorrect in exactly the way described for adapter skew, with errors growing with sequence length and layer depth. Triton-serving and Ray Serve both expose this failure in practice: Ray Serve's model update pathway (as of 2024) drains in-flight requests before swapping replicas, but this serialization means the update latency is gated on the longest in-flight context window — for long-context workloads with 32k–128k token sequences, a single slow request can block cluster-wide update propagation for tens of seconds. The cache invalidation problem is further complicated by prefix sharing across checkpoint versions: if a system like SGLang maintains a global RadixAttention trie shared across workers, a v_n block that happens to hash-match a v_{n+1} request's prefix will be returned as a cache hit even though its KV tensors are wrong, because the composite cache key must explicitly include a checkpoint version tag that most trie implementations omit. A correct implementation requires version-tagged cache namespaces — every block is stamped with (model_id, checkpoint_hash, adapter_id, quant_scheme) and lookups are filtered by exact namespace match — but this multiplies cache fragmentation proportionally to the number of simultaneously live checkpoint versions, which during a canary rollout across a large fleet can be three or four distinct versions concurrently. The cleanest operational solution used by systems like Orca and its descendants is to treat the cache as ephemeral per worker lifetime: no cross-worker or cross-version cache sharing, with the cache existing only within a single worker's memory for its current checkpoint, accepting the cold-start miss penalty on rescheduling as the price of correctness.

The key insight is that KV tensors at layer l are functions exclusively of the attention projection weights (W_Q, W_K, W_V) and the layer norm parameters feeding into them, not of the MLP weights at layer l or any subsequent layer — so if two checkpoints differ only in MLP weights, their K and V tensors are provably identical at every layer, and cross-version block sharing is mathematically safe. A system could exploit this by replacing the monolithic checkpoint hash with a per-layer attention-parameter hash: instead of tagging each block with hash(all weights), tag it with hash(W_K^l, W_V^l, γ^l, β^l) for the specific layer l that produced the block, allowing two checkpoints with identical attention weights but different MLP weights to share blocks at every layer simultaneously. The mechanism requires layer-granular cache keys — each KV block stores not a single checkpoint tag but a vector of L hashes, one per layer, and a cache lookup succeeds only if all L attention-parameter hashes match the requesting worker's current parameters — which is more expensive to compute and store but enables fine-grained sharing that the coarse checkpoint-hash approach forfeits. This is precisely the structure that would arise naturally from parameter-efficient fine-tuning auditing: if a PEFT method like LoRA only modifies W_Q and leaves W_K, W_V untouched (as some LoRA variants targeting only query projections do), then the V cache is provably reusable across the base and fine-tuned model, and a layer-hash scheme would capture this automatically without requiring the engineer to special-case it. The practical obstacle is hash computation cost: hashing all attention projection matrices at every layer on every checkpoint load adds latency proportional to the number of parameters in those matrices — for a 70B model with 80 layers, W_K and W_V together contain roughly 800M parameters, and computing a cryptographic hash over them takes non-trivial time, motivating the use of fast non-cryptographic hashes (xxHash, MurmurHash) or storing the hash alongside the checkpoint as a manifest artifact. The reintroduction risk is subtle but real: this scheme assumes MLP outputs do not feed back into the residual stream in a way that affects K/V computation at the same layer, which holds under standard Pre-LN transformer architecture but breaks under architectures with cross-layer attention or feedback connections, such as Universal Transformers or certain mixture-of-depths variants, where the MLP at layer l can influence hidden states that re-enter earlier attention computations.

The consistency guarantee required is hash-at-materialization, not hash-at-registration: the per-layer fingerprint must be computed over the fully composed matrix W_K^l + A_K^l B_K^l (where A, B are the LoRA factors) at the moment that matrix is actually used for computation, not over the base weights alone or over the adapter factors separately, because the cache block's KV tensors are a function of the composed operator and nothing else. Lazy adapter materialization — where the base weights and adapter deltas are stored separately and fused only at inference time via on-the-fly matrix multiplication — breaks this guarantee because the hash is typically computed at adapter registration time over (W_base, A, B) as separate artifacts, meaning two adapters with different (A, B) pairs that happen to produce the same composed W_K + AB^T would get different hashes and miss the cache, while conversely a system that hashes only W_base would incorrectly treat all adapters over the same base as hash-equivalent. S-LoRA's architecture (Sheng et al., 2023) exposes this directly: it stores adapter weights separately from base weights and applies them via batched GEMM at inference time, meaning the effective W_K is never materialized as a single contiguous tensor in memory, making it impossible to hash the composed matrix without explicitly computing the sum — an O(d²) operation per layer that defeats the purpose of lazy fusion. A further breakage point is adapter hot-swapping mid-request: if a system allows the adapter to change between the prefill and decode phases of a single request (as some multi-agent orchestration frameworks do to simulate persona switching), the hash computed at prefill time is no longer valid for the decode phase, but the KV blocks written during prefill are already in the cache tagged with the prefill-time hash, creating blocks whose tag is technically stale the moment the adapter changes. The correct protocol requires treating the composed attention matrix as the unit of identity and enforcing that: (1) the hash is computed over the materialized sum W_K + AB^T at the start of each forward pass, (2) adapter swaps are only permitted at sequence boundaries where no live KV blocks exist, and (3) the cache lookup gate checks the composed hash rather than any component hash — conditions that S-LoRA explicitly does not satisfy because its design priority is throughput via lazy fusion, not cache correctness under composition. The deepest guarantee failure is in quantized adapter serving: if the composed matrix W_K + AB^T is subsequently quantized to INT8 via dynamic quantization at inference time, the hash of the FP16 composed matrix does not match the hash of the INT8 result, meaning a block computed in one quantization pass cannot be safely fingerprinted by a hash computed before quantization, requiring the hash to be computed after the full materialization-and-quantization pipeline — a requirement that no current production serving system, including vLLM's LoRA serving path, implements correctly as of mid-2025.
